content.description: On **October 24, 1929**, Wall Street collapses. Within three years **25%** of Americans are out of work, and the crisis opens the way for political extremism in Europe.

hero.hook: One Thursday on Wall Street, and the world tips into a decade of misery.

blocks.text: On **October 24, 1929**, **Black Thursday**, the New York Stock Exchange collapses. This is not just a financial accident. It is the start of the **Great Depression**, a worldwide economic paralysis.
In three years, global output fell by about **15%**. Unemployment hit **25%** of Americans. European democracies tottered. Here's how one bubble swept everything away.

In the **Roaring Twenties** (the 1920s), America buys on credit: cars, radios, household appliances. Between 1920 and 1929 the **Dow Jones**, the index that tracks the price of the big American stocks, rises sixfold. The engine of the bubble: [[Buying stocks on margin]]. People borrow to buy shares, betting that they will keep rising.

blocks.caption: The Roaring Twenties: euphoria, credit and speculation

blocks.text: On the day of the crash, brokers at the Chicago exchange are said to have hanged a stork in effigy, blamed for bringing disaster instead of prosperity.

As early as 1928, production stalls and farm prices fall. Factories make more than people can buy: this is [[overproduction]]. The market is [[overvalued]], priced far above what it is really worth. When doubt spreads, everyone sells at the same time.

sections.title: The Roaring Twenties and the bubble

blocks.text: On **October 24**, eleven million sell orders. On the **29th**, “Black Tuesday,” the fall speeds up. Between 1929 and 1932 the market loses **89%** of its value. Then come the [[bank runs]]: waves of customers pulling out their money in panic. About **9,000** American banks go under.

blocks.caption: Lines of jobless men: the human face of the crisis

blocks.text: Ruined Americans hitched horses to their cars to save on gasoline. People called them “Hoover Cars,” after President [[Herbert Hoover]], judged too passive in the face of the crisis.
Without credit, factories close. Industrial output falls by about **46%**. With no welfare system worth the name, millions of people end up depending on soup kitchens.

sections.title: From the crash to the collapse of the banks

blocks.text: The United States calls its loans back home. Europe suffocates. [[The Gold Standard]], a system that ties currencies to gold, spreads the crisis: to hold on to their gold, central banks raise interest rates, which slows the economy even further.

Policies of [[deflation]] (cutting prices and wages to “clean things up”) fail. In Germany, unemployment reaches **30%**. Adolf Hitler turns the despair against [[Weimar]], the fragile German republic. In **January 1933**, he comes to power. The economic crisis opens the door to political disaster.

Elected in **1932**, **Franklin D. Roosevelt** launches [[Roosevelt's New Deal (1933)]]. That is the end of pure [[laissez-faire]], the idea that the state must never touch the market. Washington pushes for [[recovery]]: major public works, bank regulation, the first social protections. The rebound stays fragile until the war mobilization of 1941.

events.detail: Roosevelt imposes action by the state.
events.title: New Deal

blocks.text: After the crash of **1929**, the Dow Jones loses **89%** of its value, **25%** of Americans are out of work, and the crisis helps bring Hitler to power in **1933**.

content.title: The Great Depression

1933.explanation: A set of American programs combining economic stimulus (large public works), financial reform (FDIC, SEC), and social protection. It did not end the crisis, but it laid the foundations of the American welfare state.

Buying stocks on margin.explanation: Practice of borrowing from one's bank to buy shares betting on their rise. Very widespread in the 1920s, it amplified the bubble and, during the crash, forced millions of Americans to sell urgently to repay their loans.

Gold Standard.explanation: Monetary system where currencies were convertible into gold at a fixed rate, limiting the ability of states to create money. It mechanically spread the American crisis to the entire world: when the United States reduced its money supply, all countries linked to gold suffered.

Gold standard.explanation: Monetary system where currencies were convertible into gold at a fixed rate, limiting the ability of states to create money. It mechanically spread the American crisis to the entire world: when the United States reduced its money supply, all countries linked to gold suffered.

Herbert Hoover.explanation: 31st President of the United States (1929-1933), often criticized for his inability to act effectively at the onset of the crisis.

Purchasing stocks on margin.explanation: The practice of borrowing from one's bank to buy shares, betting on their rise. Very widespread in the 1920s, it amplified the bubble and, during the crash, forced millions of Americans to sell urgently to repay their loans.

Roosevelt's New Deal.explanation: A set of American programs combining economic stimulus (large public works), financial reform (FDIC, SEC), and social protection. It did not end the crisis, but it laid the foundations of the American welfare state.

Roosevelt's New Deal (1933).explanation: A set of American programs combining economic stimulus (large public works), financial reform (FDIC, SEC), and social protection. It did not end the crisis, but it laid the foundations of the American welfare state.

The Gold Standard.explanation: A monetary system where currencies were convertible into gold at a fixed rate, limiting the ability of states to create money. It mechanically spread the American crisis to the entire world: when the United States reduced their money supply, all countries linked to gold suffered.

Weimar.explanation: Republican regime in place in Germany between 1919 and 1933, destabilized by economic instability and the rise of extremes.

bank runs.explanation: When many of a bank's customers pull out their deposits at the same time for fear it will fail, and in doing so actually cause it to fail.

deflation.explanation: A generalized and lasting fall in prices and wages, which often worsens the crisis by increasing the real burden of debt.

laissez-faire.explanation: Liberal economic principle advocating for the absence of state intervention in market mechanisms.

overproduction.explanation: A situation where the supply of goods exceeds consumer demand, leading to a drop in prices and an accumulation of useless stock.

overvalued.explanation: Refers to a financial asset (stock or real estate) whose market price is significantly higher than its actual economic value.

recovery.explanation: Economic policy that tries to lift demand and production by increasing public spending.

quiz.explanation: On October 24, 1929, nicknamed Black Thursday, the New York Stock Exchange collapsed and triggered the Great Depression.

quiz.explanation: About 25% of Americans find themselves unemployed during the crisis.
quiz.question: What share of Americans were unemployed at the height of the Great Depression?

quiz.explanation: We borrow to buy shares by betting on their rise: this system of purchasing on margin multiplies losses when the market collapses.
options: Buying stocks on margin, borrowing to buy securities
Mass printing of money by the state
The continued decline in agricultural prices
quiz.question: What mechanism fueled the speculative bubble of the Roaring Twenties before the crash?

quiz.explanation: The American stock market lost approximately 89% of its value between 1929 and 1932.
quiz.question: True or false: between 1929 and 1932, the American stock market lost nearly 90% of its value.

quiz.explanation: Panicked customers rush to withdraw their money, causing around 9,000 US banks to fail.
options: Waves of customers withdrawing their money in panic
Mandatory audits imposed by the State
quiz.question: What are the “bank runs” that hit American banks after the crash?

quiz.explanation: The crash of October 1929 led to a chain of bank failures, then the crisis paved the way for Hitler and the New Deal response, both in early 1933.
items: A wave of bank failures in the United States
Hitler's rise to power in Germany
Roosevelt's launch of the New Deal
quiz.question: Put these events of the Great Depression in chronological order.

quiz.explanation: To maintain their gold reserves, European central banks raise their interest rates, which further worsens the recession.
options: The gold standard, which pushes central banks to raise their interest rates
The gold franc, the single European currency
quiz.question: Which monetary system is propagating the American economic crisis to Europe?

quiz.explanation: With 30% unemployment in Germany, Hitler exploited popular despair against the fragile Weimar Republic.
quiz.question: Who took advantage of massive unemployment in Germany to come to power in January 1933?

quiz.explanation: Elected in 1932, Roosevelt launched the New Deal: major works, banking regulation and the start of social protection, to revive the economy.
options: The New Deal, which puts an end to laissez-faire and revives the economy through the State
